author: Skye Goodman
text:
I'm proud to share that I've officially graduated from University of Bristol with a First-Class Honours MEng in Engineering Mathematics.
A highlight was achieving a 75% in my Master's dissertation, exploring how modifying the training and evaluation of state-of-the-art recurrent and transformer-based deep learning models can improve the quality of wearable health data.

I'm excited to share that this research has been accepted for publication and presentation at the ML4ITS (Machine Learning for Irregular Time Series) Workshop, held at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (https://ecmlpkdd.org/2026/ 2026) 2026. I'll be presenting this September in Naples, Italy.

ML4ITS brings together researchers developing machine learning methods for irregular time series, with applications spanning healthcare, wearable sensing, industrial monitoring, mobility and energy systems. My research focused on reconstructing missing physiological data from Garmin smartwatches collected from a participant with epilepsy, improving data quality for downstream seizure risk forecasting. More broadly, it contributes to the growing use of consumer wearable devices for continuous, non-invasive health monitoring.

A huge thank you to my brilliant supervisors and co-authors Nawid Keshtmand, Jeff Clark, Roussel Desmond Nzoyem, and Amberly Brigden for their continued mentorship and support throughout this project.

I am actively looking for ML Engineer opportunities in the space. If you're attending the conference- or if your team is hiring- I'd love to connect.
And and final huge shoutout to my best mates and fellow engineers. I couldn't have asked for a better group of people to share the last four years with, and I'm really going to miss calling Bristol home!

Choosing the “right” programming language isn’t about trends — it’s about using the right tool for the job.

Here are 5 of the most in-demand languages in today’s market, along with where they shine (and where they don’t):

—

🐍 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Simple syntax, massive ecosystem, great for automation
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Data analysis, AI/ML, scripting, backend services
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Slower performance compared to compiled languages

—

☕ 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Platform independence, strong typing, enterprise stability
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Large-scale systems, banking, Android apps
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Verbose syntax, slower development cycles

—

🟨 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Runs everywhere, huge ecosystem, full-stack capability
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Web apps, APIs, front-end + back-end (Node.js)
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Inconsistent behavior, dependency overload

—

⚙️ 𝗖++
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: High performance, low-level memory control
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Game engines, embedded systems, high-frequency trading
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Steep learning curve, memory management complexity

—

🐹 𝗚𝗼 (𝗚𝗼𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴)
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Fast, simple concurrency, easy deployment
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Cloud services, microservices, DevOps tools
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Less flexibility, smaller ecosystem than older languages

—

🔍 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆
No single language is “best.” The most effective engineers understand trade-offs and choose based on the problem — not hype.

If you're learning or hiring, focus on alignment with real-world use cases, not just popularity charts.

author: Shubham Rawat
text:
Arsenal is hiring a Research Engineer to build AI for football.

Yes, actual football. ⚽

Not an AI chatbot telling Mikel Arteta who to start 😂

The role sits directly with Arsenal’s Men’s First Team Analysis department.

And what caught my attention is what they want AI for:

Building data-driven tools for analysts and coaches.

Automating football analysis tasks.

Applying ML to real coaching and analysis problems.

Basically, AI is slowly moving from your laptop to the touchline.

And this got me thinking about how quickly AI has entered my own work.

I run an SEO agency.

A couple of years ago, most of my day would have been:

*Finding websites manually
*Checking hundreds of pages
*Researching prospects
*Writing outreach
*Finding link opportunities

Now I use AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini almost daily to help with research, analyse pages, write small scripts, automate repetitive work and find better link opportunities.

The interesting part?

AI didn't replace SEO.

It changed how I do SEO.

And I think football will be similar.

AI isn't going to replace the coach making the final call.

But the coach with better data, better tools and better information might have an advantage over the one without them.

When a football club is hiring AI engineers alongside analysts and coaches, you realise AI isn't becoming an industry anymore.

It's becoming a layer inside every industry.

Even football.
